articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India must improve ties with Bangladesh, and protect Hasina

Bangladesh’s former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina now in exile in India, has set off speculation about her imminent return to Dhaka by submitting an application for a new Bangladeshi passport and national identity card this week. The application, made through the Bangladesh High Commission in Delhi, was dismissed by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir, who said that the government in Dhaka would not grant a passport to a “terrorist”, and would seek her return via the extradition agreement as a “prisoner transfer process” with India. Ms. Hasina has already announced that she plans to return to Bangladesh in December this year, as she did after her previous stay in India in exile from 1975-1981, after the brutal assassination of her father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and nearly every other member of her family. However, the situation is considerably different now. This time, Ms. Hasina came to India in 2024 fleeing mobs of protestors that overthrew her government, and has since been convicted by a tribunal for ordering a crackdown on thousands of students, and sentenced to death. In interviews, including to The Hindu , Ms. Hasina says she hopes to return to Bangladesh to argue her case and rebuild her party, the Awami League, but that is hardly likely, given the anger against her amongst the polity, and bipartisan consensus to ban the Awami League from politics. Despite the harsh rhetoric it employs against her, the BNP government is unlikely to wish for her return, as it would have to begin execution proceedings against the 79-year-old former Prime Minister, with international opposition to such a move expected to be voluble. Not doing so would only strengthen its opposition party, the Jamaat-e-Islami, that has accused the Rahman government of soft-pedalling the issue. The government must also worry about possible protests and violence within the country in the event Ms. Hasina returns.

The situation puts the Modi government in a spot. Ever since Ms. Hasina announced plans to return, during a virtual press conference held in Delhi on August 5 this year, Delhi-Dhaka ties have been on a downslide. The government’s decision not to prevent Ms. Hasina from addressing the press, where she used the opportunity to soundly criticise PM Rahman, meant the abrupt cancellation of the Bangladesh PM’s visit. Next month, the Indo-Bangladesh Ganga Water treaty is set to expire, and talks on its extension have also become a casualty. Ms. Hasina has been an honoured guest in India, and the government cannot physically restrain her from taking the flight to Dhaka or travelling to the land border at Petrapole to cross over. Nor can it wash its hands of her situation once she crosses over. New Delhi must redouble its diplomatic efforts on improving bilateral ties while also ensuring Ms. Hasina’s welfare.

Editorial Context: In a dilemma: On Sheikh Hasina and India-Bangladesh ties. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

articles.title: New deal: On COP31 and lofty climate goals
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Nations must deliver on past promises before committing to lofty climate goals

The 31st Conference of Parties (COP) began this week in Antalya, Türkiye. Hosted by Türkiye and negotiations presided over by Australia, the run-up to the gathering saw ministerial delegations visit Fiji and Tuvalu. This was to serve as a stark reminder of the purpose of COPs, namely that it was small island nations that are most vulnerable to warming from rising greenhouse gas emissions. However, the opening days have belied this sense of urgency. Prominent world leaders, even from the European countries who as a group champion the cause most vociferously, have chosen to skip the meet. The agenda and pre-summit expectations suggest that the main concerns this year are likely to be about delivering on existing commitments such as delivering $300 billion a year by 2035, which was decided at COP29 in Baku, as well as the COP30 call to triple the adaptation finance during that interval. However, deciding how these climate funds will practically flow has been deferred to COP32. The second global stocktake, a periodic check on progress under the Paris Agreement, begins at COP31, but the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has dithered on a timeline for the next reports that will serve as the scientific push to policy makers to accelerate efforts towards keeping a rise in temperatures below 2°C, and more ambitiously 1.5°C.

The previous edition of COP30 concluded without a formal roadmap away from fossil fuels — a step back from the COP28 consensus in Dubai. There is a voluntary roadmap ahead of COP31 but it is out of the formal negotiating text. In the background of the West Asia war, the withdrawal of the United States from the Paris Agreement and financial strain writ large over Europe, funds are a challenge as evidenced in the recent Loss and Damage fund approval to Nepal of $21 million when the ask is in billions. COP31 president, Murat Kurum has laid an electrification target, which is to raise electricity’s share from 23% of total energy consumption to 35% by 2035. India has already refused to sign such a pledge and insisted on predictable climate finance, technology transfer, and nationally determined approaches to climate mitigation. These negotiations have a character of their own and deliberating nations must strive to get nations to deliver on past promises rather than commit to new lofty targets.

articles.summary: Nations must deliver on past promises before committing to lofty climate goals
articles.keyPoints:
• Nations must deliver on past promises before committing to lofty climate goals
• The 31st Conference of Parties (COP) began this week in Antalya, Türkiye. Hosted by Türkiye and negotiations presided over by Australia, the run-up to the gathering saw ministerial delegations visit Fiji and Tuvalu. This was to serve as a stark reminder of the purpose of COPs, namely that it was small island nations that are most vulnerable to warming from rising greenhouse gas emissions. However, the opening days have belied this sense of urgency. Prominent world leaders, even from the European countries who as a group champion the cause most vociferously, have chosen to skip the meet. The agenda and pre-summit expectations suggest that the main concerns this year are likely to be about delivering on existing commitments such as delivering $300 billion a year by 2035, which was decided at COP29 in Baku, as well as the COP30 call to triple the adaptation finance during that interval. However, deciding how these climate funds will practically flow has been deferred to COP32. The second global stocktake, a periodic check on progress under the Paris Agreement, begins at COP31, but the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has dithered on a timeline for the next reports that will serve as the scientific push to policy makers to accelerate efforts towards keeping a rise in temperatures below 2°C, and more ambitiously 1.5°C.
• The previous edition of COP30 concluded without a formal roadmap away from fossil fuels — a step back from the COP28 consensus in Dubai. There is a voluntary roadmap ahead of COP31 but it is out of the formal negotiating text. In the background of the West Asia war, the withdrawal of the United States from the Paris Agreement and financial strain writ large over Europe, funds are a challenge as evidenced in the recent Loss and Damage fund approval to Nepal of $21 million when the ask is in billions. COP31 president, Murat Kurum has laid an electrification target, which is to raise electricity’s share from 23% of total energy consumption to 35% by 2035. India has already refused to sign such a pledge and insisted on predictable climate finance, technology transfer, and nationally determined approaches to climate mitigation. These negotiations have a character of their own and deliberating nations must strive to get nations to deliver on past promises rather than commit to new lofty targets.

articles.title: Visions of the future: On this year’s Booker Prize
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: This year’s Booker Prize betrays an anxiety about AI’s place in society

A defining feature of the world today is that knowledge is proliferating and societies are struggling to agree on what is happening. AI models have significantly catalysed this devolution, allowing bad actors to flood spaces ranging from the research literature to public airwaves with questionable information, and drawing the attention of governments worldwide to the security implications of such a potent technology. The Booker Prize for M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything , a novel about a sense-defying alien invasion and the unsettling prospect of un-understandability it confronts humans with, effectively acknowledges the centrality of the AI question both through the book’s substance and the judges’ choice. A consequence of rampant AI use has been an assault on people’s attention span as well as the ability to make sense of new claims, so much so that reliable, verifiable meaning has become a premium entity. The novel, on the other hand, attempts to diagnose a post-meaning world in which people are only left to look inward. The Prize is also a long-overdue victory for the merits of science fiction, a genre that Harrison helped shape from the late 1960s, and one that English literature’s top honours have repeatedly overlooked. That said, the novel itself is far from being its best example, including because Harrison’s diagnosis lets technology and the practice of power off the hook for their failures.

One of the judges said she had also sought a book “only a human being could write”, but defending a novel for its ability to thumb its nose at the machines is unfair to the literary enterprise and betrays a wider public anxiety about AI, especially over the lack of consensus about its proper place in society. OpenAI has been aggravating these deliberations among mathematicians by using its machines to make headway, in record time, on problems that have been unsolved for decades, without also contributing to mathematical education and research. Anthropic , the American company known for its Claude AI model, has announced its IPO with a surprising proposed valuation of $1.4 trillion . Since much of this is pegged on speculative future demand for AI services, the same absence of consensus leaves room for investors to imagine an enormous market for Anthropic’s products and invest to help the company realise them, thus narrowing the space for society to deliberate on all competing visions of the future. And while The End of Everything , with its philosophy of pragmatic absurdism, offers poor guidance on how to keep that space open, doing so ultimately remains one of the most important unfinished tasks before the world today.

articles.title: Milking power: On the overturning of Gokul Dairy cooperative mandate
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: The overturning of the mandate in the Gokul Dairy cooperative is disturbing

Amid a nationwide outcry over electoral malpractices, with fresh evidence emerging every day, the BJP government in Maharashtra has gone a step further in overturning a popular mandate through an executive fiat. It approved changing the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act through an ordinance on November 4 — which the Governor promulgated on November 6 — with the immediate effect of facilitating the takeover of the Kolhapur District Cooperative Milk Producers’ Union, popularly known as Gokul Dairy , by the BJP and its allies. A Congress-led panel won 13 of the 25 elected seats on the board of the cooperative on October 19. Gokul, which is one of Maharashtra’s most influential cooperative institutions, has an annual turnover of around ₹4,000 crore and is linked to several lakh milk producers in western Maharashtra. The BJP had set its eyes on the cooperative sector as yet another arena of its political dominance, creating a Ministry of Cooperation under Home Minister Amit Shah. While that plan of controlling cooperatives continues to play out through various means, the overturning of an election clearly won by the Congress-led Opposition marks a new level of brazenness by the BJP, and of the impunity its actions continue to receive from the judiciary.

The Congress-backed Rajarshi Shahu Shetkari Samvichari Aghadi, led by Satej Patil, won 13 of the 25 elected seats on the Gokul board. On October 29, the election of the chairman was deadlocked after the BJP-allied members did not participate, and the meeting fell short of the required quorum of 14 members. The directors allied to the Congress and its partners subsequently declared Shashikant Patil Chuyekar as chairman, but the administration refused to recognise the election as quorum requirements had not been met. The amendment made through the ordinance allowed the government to nominate five directors to certain large cooperative institutions, with four nominees receiving voting rights. To be sure, four were nominated immediately to the Gokul board, and they voted with the BJP and its partners to elect a chairman on November 10 . The mandate of the cooperative’s members had been 13-12 in favour of the Congress and its allies, but it turned 16-13 in favour of the BJP and its partners, with the appointment of members with voting rights by the State government. Those defeated approached the Bombay High Court on November 9 to restrain the government-nominated directors from voting, but the High Court did not grant that relief. The diffidence of the judiciary in intervening in favour of democratic principles is turning out to be a matter of concern . The overturning of the popular mandate in Gokul Dairy cannot be seen as an isolated incident. It is yet another instance in a troubling pattern of state power silencing the people’s choice.

articles.summary: The overturning of the mandate in the Gokul Dairy cooperative is disturbing
articles.keyPoints:
• The overturning of the mandate in the Gokul Dairy cooperative is disturbing
• Amid a nationwide outcry over electoral malpractices, with fresh evidence emerging every day, the BJP government in Maharashtra has gone a step further in overturning a popular mandate through an executive fiat. It approved changing the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act through an ordinance on November 4 — which the Governor promulgated on November 6 — with the immediate effect of facilitating the takeover of the Kolhapur District Cooperative Milk Producers’ Union, popularly known as Gokul Dairy , by the BJP and its allies. A Congress-led panel won 13 of the 25 elected seats on the board of the cooperative on October 19. Gokul, which is one of Maharashtra’s most influential cooperative institutions, has an annual turnover of around ₹4,000 crore and is linked to several lakh milk producers in western Maharashtra. The BJP had set its eyes on the cooperative sector as yet another arena of its political dominance, creating a Ministry of Cooperation under Home Minister Amit Shah. While that plan of controlling cooperatives continues to play out through various means, the overturning of an election clearly won by the Congress-led Opposition marks a new level of brazenness by the BJP, and of the impunity its actions continue to receive from the judiciary.
• The Congress-backed Rajarshi Shahu Shetkari Samvichari Aghadi, led by Satej Patil, won 13 of the 25 elected seats on the Gokul board. On October 29, the election of the chairman was deadlocked after the BJP-allied members did not participate, and the meeting fell short of the required quorum of 14 members. The directors allied to the Congress and its partners subsequently declared Shashikant Patil Chuyekar as chairman, but the administration refused to recognise the election as quorum requirements had not been met. The amendment made through the ordinance allowed the government to nominate five directors to certain large cooperative institutions, with four nominees receiving voting rights. To be sure, four were nominated immediately to the Gokul board, and they voted with the BJP and its partners to elect a chairman on November 10 . The mandate of the cooperative’s members had been 13-12 in favour of the Congress and its allies, but it turned 16-13 in favour of the BJP and its partners, with the appointment of members with voting rights by the State government. Those defeated approached the Bombay High Court on November 9 to restrain the government-nominated directors from voting, but the High Court did not grant that relief. The diffidence of the judiciary in intervening in favour of democratic principles is turning out to be a matter of concern . The overturning of the popular mandate in Gokul Dairy cannot be seen as an isolated incident. It is yet another instance in a troubling pattern of state power silencing the people’s choice.

articles.title: Caste and class: On OBC reservation
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Exclusion of creamy layer is essential, but must be done consistently

If public resources are to dismantle both caste hierarchy and class inequality, OBC reservation should resist the notion that caste disadvantage makes economic differences among OBC families irrelevant. The ‘creamy layer’ rules are responsible for identifying those OBC members who have advanced sufficiently to no longer require affirmative action. However, the government has implemented them inconsistently. The Supreme Court in March corrected one inconsistency, that the government cannot hold the salary alone of an OBC candidate’s parent as evidence of social advancement. In Indra Sawhney (1992) , the Court upheld the government’s 27% reservation for OBC candidates in central government services if it also excluded economically advanced sections, i.e., the creamy layer, among OBCs. Following the equivalence requirement issued in 1993, the Department of Personnel & Training (DoPT) issued a “clarification” in 2004 that the government used, from around 2015, to deny dozens of OBC candidates who had cleared the Civil Services Examination their benefits because their parents’ salaries exceeded the official threshold due to pay revisions that did not always reflect changes in occupational status. The Cabinet also approved equivalence guidelines in 2017 but a parliamentary committee criticised it over a number of issues.

In Rohith Nathan (2026) , the Court rightly rejected the government’s use of the 2004 “clarification” to arbitrarily exclude OBC candidates based on their parents’ salaries alone. However, the government stalled service allocations following the 2025 examination and appealed that retrospectively applying the ruling would create administrative chaos. On November 6, the Court conceded that it had not asked the government to reopen completed selections, as it could set workers against one another while leaving government misapplication unaddressed. A proactive policy is essential now as the government must create supernumerary posts for legitimate claimants and apply the 1993 rules to pending allocations without vouchsafing these remedies for only those who can afford litigation. Access to public employment continues to be grossly unequal: per the 2024-25 DoPT Annual Report, OBC representation in central government employment was 26.3% but declined steadily towards higher positions. As the Justice G. Rohini Commission also indicated, the benefits of reservation are distributed unevenly among OBC communities. However, the report, submitted in 2023, is still not in the public domain. The coming Census includes caste enumeration but policymakers also need data on each caste’s education, occupations, assets, and landholdings. Defending redistribution among caste groups while ignoring major inequalities within them, and constraining OBC reservation assuming relatively more high-income families capture the benefits without first establishing the extent and the causes are equally difficult to justify.

articles.title: Without any rationale: On the disbanding of the Justice Kurian Joseph Committee
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India’s federal structure could have benefited from the Kurian Committee

By abruptly disbanding the Justice Kurian Joseph Committee on Union-State Relations and handing over its task to the Tamil Nadu State Law Commission, the C. Joseph Vijay government appears to have succumbed to the political impulse to reverse earlier decisions rather than being guided by any compelling rationale or necessity. This gains credence from the very grounds cited. The committee executed its mandate with scholarly rigour, seen in Part I of its report that was submitted to the then M.K. Stalin government in February. Citing the Committee’s basic character of being a “non-statutory body” is unconvincing, particularly when the Law Commission itself is established only through “executive order”. There is also no public evidence of State Law Commissions having examined or addressed issues concerning Union-State relations. The mandate “to suggest ways and means for the inter-State relations and Centre-State relations”, constitutes only one part of the broader terms of reference of the State Law Commission, reconstituted in August. Given the commission’s wider responsibilities, successive State governments had constituted high-level committees to examine conflicts involving Concurrent List subjects and recommend specific remedies. It is through such recommendations that Tamil Nadu enacted certain pieces of legislation to overcome limitations imposed by central laws, including the provision of horizontal reservation in professional course admissions for disadvantaged students. Therefore, the State’s other argument of “similarity or overlap” in the “nature and scope of the functions” entrusted to the Committee and the Commission, does not withstand close scrutiny.

In September, Leader of the Opposition Udhayanidhi Stalin, had flagged an attempt to “paralyse” the Committee’s functioning . A fair assessment of the Committee’s Part I Report reveals the breadth and depth of its dispassionate examination of issues, including State autonomy, delimitation, and the office of the Governor. Parties, barring the BJP, had largely welcomed the report. Interestingly, its contents are not even remotely at odds with the broad public ideological positioning of Mr. Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam on State rights. Besides, Prof. M. Naganathan, the Committee’s only member with an overt political association, had already resigned. The government would do well to rethink and allow it to complete its work. This would strengthen the political endeavour towards evolving a more balanced federal governance structure, facilitating harmonious Centre-State relations.

articles.title: Keralam CPI(M) suspends Elappully local secretary
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Party suspends him for six months following allegations of an extramarital relationship

The Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)] has suspended its Elappully East-1 local committee secretary Satheesh Kumar for six months following allegations of an extramarital relationship with another woman.
The woman’s husband has approached the family court here seeking divorce, alleging that the relationship had continued for several years.
According to the complaint, the husband has also alleged that Mr. Kumar threatened to kill him and their son by poisoning them.

The party leadership had earlier warned Mr. Kumar against continuing the relationship. However, he allegedly ignored the warning and continued to visit the woman, including at her house in Thrissur district. The party subsequently decided to suspend him for six months.
Suresh Kumar, an employee of the Elappully Service Cooperative Bank, has been given charge of the local committee secretary’s post in his place.
The latest action comes at a time when the CPI(M) in Palakkad is facing a major controversy over allegations against former district secretary E.N. Suresh Babu.
A woman had lodged a complaint of sexual misconduct against him with the party leadership, reportedly submitting digital evidence.

The party removed Mr. Babu from the district secretary’s post last month and appointed V. Chenthamarakshan as his successor. The party’s internal complaints committee is currently investigating the woman’s complaint, and its report is expected to guide further action.

articles.title: Manipur probe panel gets sixth extension, no sign of report yet
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Commission of Inquiry is mandated to probe the causes, extent of the violence and riots targeting members of different communities, the sequence of events and whether there were any lapses or dereliction of duty in this regard on the part of any of the responsible authorities and individuals
The three-member Commission of Inquiry (CoI) notified by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to probe the 2023 Manipur ethnic violence was given a sixth extension on Friday (November 13, 2026).
The MHA notified that the Commission constituted on June 4, 2023 “shall submit its report to the Central government as soon as possible but not later than May 20, 2027”.

The probe panel’s report is awaited even as the ethnic conflict has now spread between the Kuki and Naga communities. Since February this year, more than 60 people have been killed in Naga-Kuki clashes.

The Commission, which is now headed by former Supreme Court judge Balbir Singh Chauhan after Ajai Lamba, former Chief Justice of Gauhati High Court, resigned as the chairperson of the three-member panel in February this year, is yet to finalise its report.

Justice (retd.) Chauhan is also heading the judicial inquiry into the incident of violence that occurred in Ladakh’s Leh city on September 24, 2025 where four civilians including a Kargil war veteran were killed in police firing. The Ladakh report is yet to be submitted to the government.
Manipur’s Commission of Inquiry has received around 11,000 affidavits.
More than 300 people have been killed in the ethnic violence that erupted first between the Kuki-Zo and Meitei people on May 3, 2023. Around 60,000 people were displaced from their homes.
President’s rule was imposed in the State on February 13, 2025 and on February 4 this year. A new Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh took oath, ending Central rule.

The CoI is mandated to probe the causes, extent of the violence and riots targeting members of different communities, the sequence of events and whether there were any lapses or dereliction of duty in this regard on the part of any of the responsible authorities and individuals.

articles.title: TAS conference urges BRICS countries to join hands to tackle mental health stigma
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Panelists at the conference identified youth participation, school-based interventions, community mental healthcare and evidence-based policy reforms as key priorities

The 11th Together Against Stigma (TAS) conference, being organised by George Institute for Global Health in collaboration with Department of Psychiatry, AIIMS Delhi, and UNICEF, has called for stronger cooperation among BRICS countries to combat mental health stigma and discrimination, with a focus on improving access to inclusive mental healthcare for children, adolescents, and young people.

The conference, which is concluding on Saturday (November 13, 2026), has representatives from India, Brazil, South Africa, Kazakhstan and Malaysia. They have identified youth participation, school-based interventions, community mental healthcare and evidence-based policy reforms as key priorities.

Emphasising the principle of “Nothing About Us Without Us”, panellists said young people and persons with lived experience must have a meaningful role in framing mental health policies and challenging discrimination. Schools, they noted, could serve as critical points for early identification and intervention. Brazil’s experience of training teachers to recognise psychological distress and link students with public health services was highlighted as a model.

NIMHANS Director Y. C. Janardhan Reddy highlighted the role of the National Digital Academy in building India’s mental healthcare workforce. With 38 accredited courses and 72 programmes, the academy has trained nearly 50,000 professionals across the country, he said.

The conference also highlighted findings from The George Institute for Global Health India’s ARTEMIS study (Adolescents’ Resilience and Treatment needs for Mental health in Indian Slums) and the SATHI study among tribal communities. Both demonstrated the potential of locally tailored anti-stigma campaigns to improve attitudes towards people with mental health conditions. The interventions also helped reduce depression and anxiety among adolescents, said Y. K. Sandhya, Programme Lead, Mental Health, at the institute.
The BRICS Training Hub Network and Network of Centres of Excellence were identified as platforms for sharing research, expertise and effective interventions.
Being held at AIIMS, New Delhi, from November 12 to 14, the conference is the first edition hosted in a Global South country.

articles.title: Congress launches website to help voters check SIR deletions, seek restoration
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Announcing the initiative, Congress general secretary (organisation) K.C. Venugopal said the website, Iamvoterakshak.in, would allow citizens to verify their names and formally protest against deletions by applying for restoration

The Congress on Friday (November 13, 2026) launched a website where voters can check if their names have been deleted from electoral rolls during the special intensive revision (SIR) and register complaints seeking restoration.

Announcing the initiative, Congress general secretary (organisation) K.C. Venugopal said the website, Iamvoterakshak.in , would allow citizens to verify their names and formally protest against deletions by applying for restoration.

Before the announcement, Mr. Venugopal chaired a video conference with AICC general secretaries, in-charges, Pradesh Congress Committee (PCC) presidents, AICC secretaries and observers to review the party’s ongoing ‘Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao’ campaign against alleged electoral irregularities.
As part of the next phase of the campaign, Congress workers will function as ‘Vote Rakshaks’ and visit every polling booth to verify deletions from electoral rolls.

“The mission to stop ‘vote chori’ continues in every single corner of India,” Mr. Venugopal said, asserting that the Congress would continue its campaign until the integrity of the electoral system was restored.
The party will organise village-level chaupals across the country by December 15, where names deleted during the SIR exercise will be read out, Mr. Venugopal said.
The PCCs will organise large-scale ‘Samvidhan Raksha Marches’ in their respective States on November 26, Constitution Day.

articles.title: India's exports up 29.9% in October; trade deficit narrows to $20.09 billion
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The growth in India’s merchandise exports in October, the fastest in five years and faster than import growth, indicates that volumes of exports are growing along with prices
India’s merchandise exports rose to an all-time high of $49.5 billion in October 2026, bringing down the country’s overall trade deficit, official data released on Friday showed.
While a large part of this growth was due to petroleum products, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said diversification of exports to various locations helped improve the numbers.
India’s total exports, including goods and services, stood at $89.99 billion in October 2026, up nearly 30% from last October.
The overall trade deficit shrank from $25.1 billion last October to $20.1 billion year-on-year.

“In the month of October, the exports of merchandise exports have registered a new peak of $49.47 billion,” Mr. Agrawal said at a press briefing. “This is the highest-ever monthly merchandise export value, along with the highest monthly growth of 45.03% in the last five years.”
Merchandise imports rose to a record high of $89.35 billion in October 2026, up 16.5% YoY. Total imports stood at $110.1 billion, a 16.6% increase.

According to trade experts, goods exports growing faster than merchandise imports shows that while the rise in global prices contributed to the increase in the value of India’s exports, there was also an increase in the underlying export volumes.

“The particularly encouraging part of this growth is that this is not in any particular sector, this is not in any particular geography, it is broad-based across countries and regions,” Mr. Agrawal added. “43 of our 50 top export destinations posted positive growth in October 2026 as compared to 2025.”
The data show that India’s exports to 12 out of its top 20 export destinations grew by double digits or more.
Mr. Agrawal pointed out that India’s exports to its free trade agreement (FTA) partners had grown strongly.

articles.title: Why RBI wants to cap select overseas remittances at ₹50 Lakh to save rupees | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The RBI has reportedly proposed a ₹50 lakh sub-limit within the $250,000 annual Liberalised Remittance Scheme cap to curb dollar outflows and protect the rupee

The story so far: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reportedly proposed to the Ministry of Finance tightening the limits of the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), in an attempt likely aimed at preventing a massive outflow of dollars from India. Under the current structure, Indian residents can remit up to $250,000 (over ₹2 crore) in a financial year for purposes such as travel, education, medical treatment, and overseas investments.

The LRS is a scheme under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), introduced by the RBI in 2004. It covers both capital account and current account transactions. Under the capital account, transactions are permitted for opening overseas foreign currency bank accounts, purchasing property, extending interest-free loans of up to one year, and investing in foreign equity, mutual funds, and listed debt securities.

articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Rampur Bushahr’s Lavi Fair in Himachal Pradesh traces a Himalayan journey from wool and barter to women entrepreneurs and digital payments

What Disneyland is to children today, Lavi Fair in Rampur Bushahr, in Himachal Pradesh’s Shimla district, was to my family in the 1980s. I recall wandering through the fair as an eight-year-old, watching an old man smoking a chillum beside heaps of black sheep fleece and stacks of white woollen pattus (traditional garments of Kinnaur and Kullu women).

Mother and her friends carefully chose shawls for their daughters’ and future daughters-in-law’s trousseaux. Years later, I received a beautiful black sheep wool and pashmina shawl for my wedding. Wool finds pride of place at the fair. The name Lavi is linked to “Loe”, a sheet of woollen cloth and the practice of shearing sheep.

articles.title: How did a tax proposal lead the Dutch government to the verge of collapse? | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The Netherlands currently has a minority government by a coalition of three parties holding 66 seats in the 150-member Tweede Kamer, the lower house

Story so far: The Dutch government came close to a collapse this week over its Tax Plan for 2027 as members of the three-party ruling coalition disagreed over an amendment to the plan. Though the plan was passed in the lowest-possible majority in the House of Representatives on Thursday (November 12, 2026) night and the government subsequently defeated a no-confidence motion, the developments have brought a rift in the coalition out in the open and threaten the future of the government led by Rob Jetten just nine-months into its 4-year term.

The Netherlands currently has a minority government by a coalition of three parties holding 66 seats in the 150-member Tweede Kamer, the lower house. The centrist D66 led by Prime Minister Jetten, the youngest premier in the country’s history, is the single largest party with 26 seats and is joined by centre-right parties People’s Party for Freedom and Democracy (VVD) and Christian Democratic Appeal (CDA), with 22 and 18 seats respectively. The government came to power in February, 117 days after a snap election in October last year necessitated by the collapse of Dick Schoof’s right-wing government as far-right leader of Freedom Party Geert Wilders withdrew his support. The months following the election that failed to produce a clear winner saw parties across political spectrum and ideologies negotiate to form a government to no effect, paving the way for the centrist parties to make do with a minority administration.

Though the plan was passed in the lowest-possible majority in the House of Representatives on Thursday (November 12, 2026) night and the government subsequently defeated a no-confidence motion, the developments have brought a rift in the coalition out in the open and threaten the future of the government led by Rob Jetten just nine-months into its 4-year term.

The centrist D66 led by Prime Minister Jetten, the youngest premier in the country’s history, is the single largest party with 26 seats and is joined by centre-right parties People’s Party for Freedom and Democracy (VVD) and Christian Democratic Appeal (CDA), with 22 and 18 seats respectively. The government came to power in February, 117 days after a snap election in October last year necessitated by the collapse of Dick Schoof’s right-wing government as far-right leader of Freedom Party Geert Wilders withdrew his support. The months following the election that failed to produce a clear winner saw parties across political spectrum and ideologies negotiate to form a government to no effect, paving the way for the centrist parties to make do with a minority administration.

articles.title: CAG widens purview of power sector audit, starting with DISCOMs; consumer satisfaction in focus
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Officials stated that DISCOMs would be evaluated for their performance over a five-year period, following by transmission, generation, renewable energy and RDSS.

The Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) is undertaking a comprehensive audit of the power sector, beginning with distribution companies (discoms), where consumer satisfaction, power trading and financial sustainability emerging as key focus areas.

The exercise will subsequently cover transmission, generation, renewable energy and the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), with each segment’s operational and financial performance being assessed over the preceding five years, according to officials familiar with the development.

Discoms will be the first to be audited, with the ongoing phase covering their performance between FY21 and FY26. As many as 39 discoms across the country, along with five departmental undertakings, will be assessed. Privately owned discoms, however, will remain outside the scope of the exercise.
The audit commenced in July this year, with the report expected to be finalised around the middle of the next financial year. The audit of the transmission segment is scheduled to begin with FY27.
Moving beyond conventional financial and operational assessments, the CAG has directed auditors to engage directly with electricity consumers, local experts and influential groups..
“We told our auditors that it (the audit) must not be limited to a stakeholder consultation exercise, we must engage with consumers of electricity,” an official said.
The exercise will capture the experiences of around 10,000 consumers across industrial, agricultural and domestic categories, with particular emphasis on the reliability and quality of power supply.

Power trading and procurement costs will constitute another major area of scrutiny. Officials pointed out that the share of short-term power procurement in states’ overall power purchase basket has risen from around 7-8% five years ago to nearly 14% currently, with power exchanges accounting for more than 56% of such transactions.
“Ultimately, the cost at which the power is purchased would impact the end consumer of the electricity, and it also impacts financials of the entities concerned,” officials said.

The audit will also examine key operational indicators, including aggregate technical and commercial (AT&C) losses, billing and collection efficiency, alongside the financial health and long-term viability of discoms.

articles.title: Ukraine fires nearly 1,200 drones at Russia as U.S.-led talks consider wider European security
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Kyiv's forces are using drones and ground robots to help defend against Russia's army along the about 1,200-km front line snaking down eastern and southeastern Ukraine
Ukraine fired almost 1,200 drones at Russian targets overnight in one of its biggest aerial attacks since Moscow's invasion nearly five years ago.

Meanwhile, negotiators raised the stakes in talks to stop the fighting by including for discussion wider European security arrangements that have been in place since the end of the Cold War. That has alarmed European leaders and placed a question mark over NATO's future role.

After two days of talks with Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi this week, U.S. envoys went in person to brief Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was meeting with European Union leaders in Dublin, Ireland.
Further talks are planned as negotiators seek a breakthrough in peace efforts, according to U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump's son-in-law.
Mr. Kushner said Russia has agreed to include Europe in upcoming talks, after Moscow's long insistence that the continent's governments were part of the problem because they were supporting Ukraine.

Europe's presence at the negotiating table will allow negotiators “to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Mr. Kushner said on X.
As European leaders scrambled to find an envoy to the talks, they were also wary of Russian maneuvering as well as Mr. Trump's praise for Mr. Putin and his administration's sharp criticism of Europe.
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said on Friday (November 13, 2026) that Europe must insist on a ceasefire before taking the negotiations further — the opposite of what Mr. Putin demands.
“If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us,” she said in Dublin.
Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden insisted that Europe must take its fate into its own hands.

🎯 Exam Relevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy

Kyiv's forces are using drones and ground robots to help defend against Russia's army along the about 1,200-km front line snaking down eastern and southeastern Ukraine

Ukraine fired almost 1,200 drones at Russian targets overnight in one of its biggest aerial attacks since Moscow's invasion nearly five years ago.

Meanwhile, negotiators raised the stakes in talks to stop the fighting by including for discussion wider European security arrangements that have been in place since the end of the Cold War. That has alarmed European leaders and placed a question mark over NATO's future role.

After two days of talks with Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi this week, U.S. envoys went in person to brief Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was meeting with European Union leaders in Dublin, Ireland.

Further talks are planned as negotiators seek a breakthrough in peace efforts, according to U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

Mr. Kushner said Russia has agreed to include Europe in upcoming talks, after Moscow's long insistence that the continent's governments were part of the problem because they were supporting Ukraine.

Europe's presence at the negotiating table will allow negotiators “to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Mr. Kushner said on X.

As European leaders scrambled to find an envoy to the talks, they were also wary of Russian maneuvering as well as Mr. Trump's praise for Mr. Putin and his administration's sharp criticism of Europe.

The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said on Friday (November 13, 2026) that Europe must insist on a ceasefire before taking the negotiations further — the opposite of what Mr. Putin demands.

“If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us,” she said in Dublin.

Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden insisted that Europe must take its fate into its own hands.

articles.title: Armed men kill at least 37 civilians in western Niger, say local sources
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy

articles.title: Syria removes visa restrictions on U.S. travellers after backlash
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The current Syrian government, in place since Islamist-led fighters overthrew Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, has allowed Westerners to obtain entry visas at Damascus airport or border crossings
Syria has lifted restrictions on the entry of U.S. citizens imposed several days ago, an official told AFP on Friday (November 13, 2026), after the limits sparked uproar online.
The current Syrian government, in place since Islamist-led fighters overthrew Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, has allowed Westerners to obtain entry visas at Damascus airport or border crossings.
However, this week, several U.S. citizens complained on social media that they had been turned away on the grounds they needed a visa in advance.

"The entry procedures for U.S. citizens travelling to Syria have returned to their earlier state, after the cancellation of the obligation to obtain prior authorisation, which was imposed temporarily by the interior ministry," Mazen Allouch, an official with the ports and borders authority, told AFP .
He said there had been no change for citizens of other countries, including Europeans.

According to Syria's Tourism Ministry, 719,000 tourists, excluding travellers from Arab nations, visited the country in the first six months of 2026, despite its struggles to recover from more than a decade of civil war and the sectarian and ethnic tensions that followed its end.
That figure was a sharp increase on the number from 2025, which was just 131,000.
International flights have resumed to Syria, while Western nations including the United States have lifted sanctions imposed on Damascus during the Assad years in an effort to help it rebuild.

articles.title: Microsoft Outage LIVE: Microsoft apologises for outage, says it was not linked to cyber or AI
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Microsoft services are beginning to come back online after a massive global outage left millions of users without access for nearly 18 hours

The story so far: Software giant Microsoft is facing a widespread outage affecting users of its Outlook email service, as well as its other workplace products. Thousands of Microsoft users in India awakened on Friday (November 13, 2026) to find their inboxes inaccessible, losing hours of productivity. According to DownDetector, over 100,000 users had initially registered complaints about Microsoft Outlook.​ Microsoft Outage: Why did Microsoft Outlook and other products go offline globally? Microsoft shared on X on November 13 that a portion of infrastructure was experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, and this could likely be contributing to the connectivity errors. ​
Microsoft shared on X on November 13 that a portion of infrastructure was experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, and this could likely be contributing to the connectivity errors.

Microsoft, in a post on X, said it was “deeply sorry” for the disruption and was seeing “broad recovery and stability” across its services. It said the outage was a technical issue “not related to cyber or AI / agents”, introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a recent network change.
It said services were restored gradually, validating stability at each stage, and promised a full post-incident report once its review is complete.
IndiGo said its email support services have been impacted by the Microsoft service disruption. In a post on X, the country’s largest airline said all other support channels remain available.
“Due to a global Microsoft service disruption, our email support services are currently impacted, and we may not be able to receive your emails,” the carrier said.

Microsoft 365 has reported improving service availability and email delivery performance across affected infrastructure, adding that there is no indication that the outage was caused by malicious or cyber activity.
The company said its teams are reviewing the incident and working to prevent similar disruptions in the future.

Microsoft says service availability is improving, with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels. However, some users may continue to face intermittent access issues and delayed email delivery as the company restores affected infrastructure and monitors recovery.
Microsoft said it was seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with broader improvements in North America and across much of Europe.

articles.title: Pakistan calls for 'immediate' end to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia at UN
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: UN Security Council renewed targeted sanctions under its Yemen sanctions regime for another year

Pakistan has called for the “immediate and unconditional” cessation of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as the UN Security Council renewed targeted sanctions under its Yemen sanctions regime for another year.
The Security Council unanimously adopted the resolution on Thursday (November 12, 2026).

According to a report in Dawn , Pakistan's Permanent Representative to the UN Ambassador Syed Haider Shah, while explaining his country's vote in favour of the resolution, said that Islamabad “condemns in the strongest terms” the continued Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia.

The Iran-backed Houthis have intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, claiming strikes on oil infrastructure and military facilities, while Saudi air defences have intercepted several missiles and drones, including those targeting Riyadh.

“We stand in full and unwavering solidarity with the leadership, government, and brotherly people of Saudi Arabia. Our support for the kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, security and stability is resolute,” Mr. Shah said.

“Consistent with the United Nations Charter and international law, we support its legitimate right to defend its territory and protect its citizens and residents. We demand an immediate and unconditional cessation of these reprehensible Houthi attacks,” he said.
Mr. Shah described accountability for individuals and entities threatening Yemen’s peace, security, and stability as essential to creating conditions for lasting peace.

The resolution condemns Houthi military escalation inside Yemen, cross-border attacks against Saudi Arabia, and threats to commercial shipping, and seeks to address the group's access to dual-use components and precursor chemicals used in weapons production, the report said.

Pakistan backed stronger international action against the Houthis but stressed that the conflict required a political settlement respecting Yemen's sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity.

Mr. Shah called for an inclusive political process under UN leadership, saying an “inclusive political process that is Yemeni-owned and Yemeni-led” was necessary to advance peace and stability, as he reaffirmed Pakistan's readiness to support international efforts to restore peace and stability and address Yemen's humanitarian suffering.

UN Security Council renewed targeted sanctions under its Yemen sanctions regime for another year

Pakistan has called for the “immediate and unconditional” cessation of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as the UN Security Council renewed targeted sanctions under its Yemen sanctions regime for another year.

The Security Council unanimously adopted the resolution on Thursday (November 12, 2026).

According to a report in Dawn , Pakistan's Permanent Representative to the UN Ambassador Syed Haider Shah, while explaining his country's vote in favour of the resolution, said that Islamabad “condemns in the strongest terms” the continued Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia.

The Iran-backed Houthis have intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, claiming strikes on oil infrastructure and military facilities, while Saudi air defences have intercepted several missiles and drones, including those targeting Riyadh.

“We stand in full and unwavering solidarity with the leadership, government, and brotherly people of Saudi Arabia. Our support for the kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, security and stability is resolute,” Mr. Shah said.

“Consistent with the United Nations Charter and international law, we support its legitimate right to defend its territory and protect its citizens and residents. We demand an immediate and unconditional cessation of these reprehensible Houthi attacks,” he said.

Mr. Shah described accountability for individuals and entities threatening Yemen’s peace, security, and stability as essential to creating conditions for lasting peace.

The resolution condemns Houthi military escalation inside Yemen, cross-border attacks against Saudi Arabia, and threats to commercial shipping, and seeks to address the group's access to dual-use components and precursor chemicals used in weapons production, the report said.

Pakistan backed stronger international action against the Houthis but stressed that the conflict required a political settlement respecting Yemen's sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity.

Mr. Shah called for an inclusive political process under UN leadership, saying an “inclusive political process that is Yemeni-owned and Yemeni-led” was necessary to advance peace and stability, as he reaffirmed Pakistan's readiness to support international efforts to restore peace and stability and address Yemen's humanitarian suffering.

articles.title: Microsoft outage hits businesses worldwide; India feels impact
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Disruption to Microsoft’s cloud-based email service affects business operations and airline customer support in India; public services in several countries also report problems

The global disruption of multiple Microsoft services, which began on Thursday (November 12, 2026) and continued late into Friday (November 13, 2026), affected several Indian businesses’ internal communications and customer-facing operations.

In its latest update on Friday (November 13, 2026), the company said it was making progress in fixing the outage, which has affected email access and workplace applications in businesses, public services, and other organisations across the globe. In India, the disruptions affected businesses from stratups to multinational corporations.

A senior executive at a major telecom company in India told The Hindu that employees were unable to access emails or send service-disruption alerts to customers. Call-centre traffic also increased, the executive said.

Rahul Ganapathy, co-founder and CEO of deep tech startup Atsuya Technologies, said customer emails and scheduled Teams meetings were disrupted, although his company did not rely entirely on Microsoft internally.
At a Big Four professional services firm in Bengaluru, a senior employee said its internal operations were affected, but added that IT teams were restoring services.
The disruptions also left airlines experiencing customer-support delays.

IndiGo said its email support was affected and advised customers to use 6E Skai, its AI-powered virtual assistant. Akasa Air warned of email support delays and directed passengers to its customer care centre and social media. Air India said flight operations were unaffected, although it rerouted emails.

Separately, India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, issued a high-severity advisory on Friday, warning of multiple vulnerabilities in Microsoft products. It flagged an Outlook vulnerability that it said was being actively exploited and urged users to apply security updates. The advisory did not explicitly link the vulnerabilities to the outage.

Microsoft identified Exchange Online — described as its cloud-based messaging platform that delivers email, calendar, contacts, and tasks — as the primary service affected. Some Microsoft Graph requests accessing Exchange Online data timed out, affecting dependent features in Teams, Copilot, and SharePoint, the company said. Core Teams messaging and online meetings largely continued normally, it added.

On Friday, Microsoft said recovery was progressing, with improvements in North America and Europe and encouraging signs in Asia-Pacific. Service availability and email delivery were improving, but intermittent access problems and delays could continue, it said, adding that it was working through email backlogs and retained a 48-hour timeout window to protect delayed messages. Service health and capacity had not fully returned to baseline, it said.

fullParagraphs: Microsoft services are beginning to come back online after a massive global outage left millions of users without access for nearly 18 hours

Thousands of Microsoft users in India awakened on Friday (November 13, 2026) to find their inboxes inaccessible, losing hours of productivity. According to DownDetector, over 100,000 users had initially registered complaints about Microsoft Outlook.​ Microsoft Outage: Why did Microsoft Outlook and other products go offline globally? Microsoft shared on X on November 13 that a portion of infrastructure was experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, and this could likely be contributing to the connectivity errors. ​
Microsoft shared on X on November 13 that a portion of infrastructure was experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, and this could likely be contributing to the connectivity errors.

Microsoft, in a post on X, said it was “deeply sorry” for the disruption and was seeing “broad recovery and stability” across its services. It said the outage was a technical issue “not related to cyber or AI / agents”, introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a recent network change.
It said services were restored gradually, validating stability at each stage, and promised a full post-incident report once its review is complete.
IndiGo said its email support services have been impacted by the Microsoft service disruption. In a post on X, the country’s largest airline said all other support channels remain available.
“Due to a global Microsoft service disruption, our email support services are currently impacted, and we may not be able to receive your emails,” the carrier said.

Microsoft 365 has reported improving service availability and email delivery performance across affected infrastructure, adding that there is no indication that the outage was caused by malicious or cyber activity.
The company said its teams are reviewing the incident and working to prevent similar disruptions in the future.

Microsoft says service availability is improving, with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels. However, some users may continue to face intermittent access issues and delayed email delivery as the company restores affected infrastructure and monitors recovery.
Microsoft said it was seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with broader improvements in North America and across much of Europe.

articles.title: Telangana Women’s Commission issues notices to eight ART centres in illegal oocyte racket case
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The Telangana State Women’s Commission (TGSCW) has initiated an inquiry into an alleged illegal oocyte donation racket in Hyderabad, issuing notices to eight Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) centres and egg banks over suspected irregularities in their donor records and procurement practices.

The Commission examined representatives of the eight institutions on Friday, November 13, after directing their managements to appear before it. However, TGSCW Chairperson Nerella Sharada expressed dissatisfaction after some centres sent staff members and other representatives instead of senior management, despite being specifically instructed to attend in person. The inquiry was subsequently adjourned after the institutions assured the Commission that their management would appear at the next hearing.

During Friday’s proceedings, the Commission scrutinised reports, records and details of egg donors submitted by the ART centres and egg banks. “Several irregularities and suspicious elements have emerged from the records examined so far,” said Ms. Sharada.

She also questioned claims made by the institutions that nearly 90% of their egg donors came from other States and donated their eggs voluntarily without receiving any remuneration or financial compensation. She said the claims raised several questions and warranted further investigation.

Commissioner of Health and Family Welfare, Sangeetha Satyanarayana, also attended the inquiry, during which Ms. Sharada sought details about the progress of the department’s investigation into the alleged illegal egg procurement practices. The discussions also covered shortcomings in the existing Assisted Reproductive Technology Act and its implementation, particularly the challenges in regulating and monitoring ART centres and egg banks.

Ms. Sharada said she would soon meet Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha and Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy to inform them of the findings and discuss corrective measures, including possible legislative amendments to strengthen regulation of the sector.

Ms. Sharada further said that the Commission has also received information indicating the possible involvement of several other ART centres and egg banks in the alleged racket. It plans to issue notices to their management and summon them for questioning as part of the ongoing inquiry.

“The Commission will not tolerate illegal practices that compromise women’s health, dignity and rights. We will continue the investigation in coordination with the concerned government departments to identify those responsible and ensure appropriate legal action,” she added.

articles.title: As external funding to combat TB falls, domestic spending accounts for 86%: WHO report
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: TB cases remain one of the leading causes of death from a single infectious agent, with a quarter of all cases concentrated in India in 2025

Around 86% of the spending on measures against tuberculosis (TB) in 2025 came from domestic sources, the recently released Global Tuberculosis Report 2026 by the World Health Organisation (WHO) said, even as the reduction in international donor funding to combat the infectious disease remains a cause of concern.

TB cases remain one of the leading causes of death from a single infectious agent, with a quarter of all cases concentrated in India in 2025. The report notes that $22 billion is needed annually for TB prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care to achieve the global targets agreed on at the 2023 United Nations high-level TB meeting by 2027.

articles.title: Aaditya Thackeray calls for Climate Change Councils at Centre, State levels to tackle pollution
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: At the State level, he proposed similar councils chaired by the respective Chief Ministers, with participation from relevant departments to monitor the implementation of climate action plans

Shiv Sena (UBT) leader and former Maharashtra Environment Minister Aaditya Thackeray has called for the establishment of Climate Change Councils at the Central and State levels, modelled on the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council, to ensure coordinated action against pollution and climate change.

In a post on X on Thursday, November 12, Mr. Thackeray criticised the Centre over deteriorating environmental conditions across the country and accused it of presenting misleading statistics and engaging in “greenwashing” rather than addressing the crisis.

He proposed that a central Climate Change Council be chaired by the Prime Minister and include Environment Ministers from all States. The council, he suggested, should meet every three months to review environmental data, climate targets and the progress made towards achieving them.

Mr. Thackeray also recommended including Union Ministers and representatives from departments such as urban development, rural development, energy, agriculture, industry and roads, depending on the issues under discussion.
At the State level, he proposed similar councils chaired by the respective Chief Ministers, with participation from relevant departments to monitor the implementation of climate action plans.

Referring to the ongoing COP31 climate conference in Türkiye and upcoming environmental events in Mumbai, including the Earthshot Prize and Mumbai Climate Week, Mr. Thackeray questioned the Centre’s commitment to fulfilling its international climate obligations.
He alleged that discrepancies between official environmental statistics and actual conditions had affected India’s standing on international climate indices.

Highlighting the impact of pollution on citizens, Mr. Thackeray said people were increasingly being forced to spend their own money on air purifiers, water purifiers and access to safe food despite paying direct and indirect taxes.

He also claimed that worsening environmental conditions were forcing some citizens to relocate and prompting businesses to consider leaving the country, potentially affecting employment opportunities.
Mr. Thackeray questioned whether the government was adequately addressing citizens’ basic needs, including access to clean air, safe drinking water and uncontaminated food.

articles.title: Cracker conundrum: On need for strict enforcement of cracker ban
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Any regulation of crackers needs strict enforcement at all levels

The two Deepavali nights following the Supreme Court’s (SC) temporary relaxation of the cracker ban , played out predictably. The Air Quality Index (AQI) in several north Indian cities — already ‘poor’ and ‘very poor’ in the first week of November — was ‘severe’ on Deepavali night . Several air sensors — maintained by various organisations — reported PM2.5 in Delhi and its outskirts, exceeding 1,000 by Deepavali night. In this context, the SC’s order last week regarding crackers bears revisiting. While stating it was aware of the consequences of emissions from crackers, the Court has been waiting for quantitative evidence on the health and environmental effects of emissions from Deepavali celebrations. Such direct, causative evidence is almost impossible to furnish. Slackening winds and post-monsoon atmospheric dryness are known to trap the latent particulate matter from vehicles, industries, construction dust and stubble burning. Crackers are only an additional element that further degrades an already vitiated air. Delhi’s five-day average AQI rose from approximately 298 before Deepavali to 358 afterwards in 2024, 259 to 315 in 2025 and from 350 to 376 in 2026. While the timing of these spikes is consistent with a contribution from firecrackers, their precise share of overall pollution cannot be isolated from other emissions and meteorological influences. An absolute ban would encourage “illegal crackers from across the border,” the Court was told. Cracker season begins a fortnight before Deepavali and therefore an earlier decision by the Court regarding its permissibility would have given stockists time to better dispense ‘green’ crackers.

However, it is important to note that CSIR-NEERI, the developers of the products, underline that low-emission crackers — under stringent lab conditions — only reduce emissions by 30%–45%. These percentage reductions reveal nothing about gross particulate matter emissions. The post-Deepavali AQI is evidence of this. The Court acknowledges, but does not address, the immense implementation challenges in policing cracker sales and hyphenates crackers with religious observation but pays only lip service to provisions in the Constitution that say that religious customs cannot override considerations of health and life. Rather than wait for the week running up to Deepavali 2027, the Court must pronounce a final view on crackers and lay down the contours for the government to evolve a policy on limiting the manufacture, sale, and burning of crackers in a time-bound manner.

Editorial Context: Cracker conundrum: On need for strict enforcement of cracker ban. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

Any regulation of crackers needs strict enforcement at all levels

The two Deepavali nights following the Supreme Court’s (SC) temporary relaxation of the cracker ban , played out predictably. The Air Quality Index (AQI) in several north Indian cities — already ‘poor’ and ‘very poor’ in the first week of November — was ‘severe’ on Deepavali night . Several air sensors — maintained by various organisations — reported PM2.5 in Delhi and its outskirts, exceeding 1,000 by Deepavali night. In this context, the SC’s order last week regarding crackers bears revisiting. While stating it was aware of the consequences of emissions from crackers, the Court has been waiting for quantitative evidence on the health and environmental effects of emissions from Deepavali celebrations. Such direct, causative evidence is almost impossible to furnish. Slackening winds and post-monsoon atmospheric dryness are known to trap the latent particulate matter from vehicles, industries, construction dust and stubble burning. Crackers are only an additional element that further degrades an already vitiated air. Delhi’s five-day average AQI rose from approximately 298 before Deepavali to 358 afterwards in 2024, 259 to 315 in 2025 and from 350 to 376 in 2026. While the timing of these spikes is consistent with a contribution from firecrackers, their precise share of overall pollution cannot be isolated from other emissions and meteorological influences. An absolute ban would encourage “illegal crackers from across the border,” the Court was told. Cracker season begins a fortnight before Deepavali and therefore an earlier decision by the Court regarding its permissibility would have given stockists time to better dispense ‘green’ crackers.

However, it is important to note that CSIR-NEERI, the developers of the products, underline that low-emission crackers — under stringent lab conditions — only reduce emissions by 30%–45%. These percentage reductions reveal nothing about gross particulate matter emissions. The post-Deepavali AQI is evidence of this. The Court acknowledges, but does not address, the immense implementation challenges in policing cracker sales and hyphenates crackers with religious observation but pays only lip service to provisions in the Constitution that say that religious customs cannot override considerations of health and life. Rather than wait for the week running up to Deepavali 2027, the Court must pronounce a final view on crackers and lay down the contours for the government to evolve a policy on limiting the manufacture, sale, and burning of crackers in a time-bound manner.

articles.title: Point of no return: On Israel’s next government
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Without peace, Israel risks descending into chaos

Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s decision to invite opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government reflects the real mandate of the October 27 legislative elections. While Mr. Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party finished second with 21 seats, behind Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud, which won 27, the former military chief, who campaigned on an anti-Netanyahu platform, has secured the support of 67 legislators in the 120-member Knesset. In Mr. Eisenkot’s own words, Israel risks “descending to dark places, to a point of no return”. But it is not yet clear what kind of a government Mr. Eisenkot is seeking to form. The opposition parties are split between a Jewish-led bloc with 48 MKs and an Arab-led bloc of 19 MKs. Arab parties have offered in-principle support for Mr. Eisenkot to keep Mr. Netanyahu’s right-religious coalition out of power. But what is not clear is whether they would be part of the government or offer outside support by allowing Mr. Eisenkot to run a minority government. Some of Mr. Eisenkot’s Jewish right-wing allies, such as Avigdor Lieberman, are opposed to joining hands with Arab parties. Mr. Eisenkot has now called for a unity government, appealing even to Likud and the far-right Religious Zionism, to join him.

But the challenges facing Israel’s next leader are formidable and immediate. Mr. Netanyahu’s unchecked militarism has deepened Israel’s international isolation, strained its relationship with the U.S., its most important patron and ally, and aggravated the security challenges it faces in its neighbourhood. At home, the surge of the far-right has further polarised society, while systemic violence against Palestinians has spread across the West Bank. Mr. Netanyahu’s response to these challenges has been to unleash more violence, which has only compounded Israel’s problems. If Mr. Eisenkot is serious about pulling Israel back from the point of no return, he must pursue a three-pronged approach. Firstly, he should form an Arab-Jewish unity government focused on healing the country’s internal wounds and bridging gaps between communities. Second, Israel’s deepening international isolation and increasingly negative public opinion around the world will begin to exact a heavy toll sooner rather than later. Tel Aviv must take urgent steps to restore its international standing. Third, Israel must reopen the path to peace. The new government should initiate negotiations with the Palestinians under international mediation, crack down on settler violence, pull back from Gaza and reaffirm its commitment to the two-state solution. Without peace, Israel risks continuing to “descend to dark places”.
Editorial Context: Point of no return: On Israel’s next government. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.
